analysis.one_liner: Bars automakers from selling drivers' vehicle data and gives owners free control of it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 18, 2024, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and died there two weeks later when the Congress ended, without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop car and truck makers from collecting or selling the data their vehicles generate — location, driving behavior, internet activity — unless the owner gives clear, written, revocable consent. It would also require manufacturers to give owners free, open access to their own vehicle data, allow them to delete their data, and make it a federal trade violation to sell Americans' vehicle data to China, Russia, North Korea, Iran, or Venezuela. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and owners of cars, trucks, and farm or construction equipment. Modern vehicles record where you go, how you drive, and sometimes what you do online. Under this bill, that data could not be accessed or sold without the owner's affirmative written consent (except to improve vehicle safety or performance, or under a warrant, court order, or emergency), owners could get and control their own data at no extra cost, and they could delete data they generated. Independent repair shops would also benefit, because owners could access and share their vehicle's data without paying a manufacturer for decryption tools or using manufacturer-only devices [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Would require a vehicle owner's freely given, informed, written, revocable consent before a manufacturer may access the data the vehicle generates, with only narrow exceptions for improving vehicle performance or safety, warrants, court orders with 48 hours' notice to object, and emergencies.

Would generally prohibit manufacturers from selling, leasing, or sharing vehicle operator data, and would flatly ban selling Americans' vehicle data — including location and internet activity — to North Korea, China, Russia, Iran, or Venezuela.

Would require manufacturers to give owners access to and control of their vehicle's data at no cost beyond the purchase price, with no fee to decrypt it and no requirement to use manufacturer-provided devices, and would require open interfaces so owners can delete their own data and set their own preferences.

Would make violations enforceable by the FTC as unfair or deceptive practices, and would require the FTC to report to Congress within 180 days on who is accessing vehicle data, where it is sold, and how often it has been compromised.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would lose the ability to monetize the data their connected vehicles generate, would have to build open, secure, technology-neutral data interfaces at their own expense (the bill allows no new FTC appropriations, so the agency would have to do the work from existing funds), and could not charge owners for decryption or access tools [S2]. Companies that buy telematics data — brokers, insurers, and marketers — would lose their supply of driver data [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state law: Section 7 says it supersedes any state statute or rule relating to its requirements, which could override stronger state vehicle-privacy protections (such as California's) with a single federal floor.

The consent rules have a broad carve-out: manufacturers may access operator data without consent whenever it is 'solely to improve covered vehicle performance or safety,' a term the bill does not define, which could swallow much of the protection.

Only the FTC could enforce the bill; there is no private right of action for individual drivers, and the FTC is directed to do the reporting and standards-setting work with no new appropriations, stretching existing agency resources.
The FTC would have up to a year after its initial report to set the required data-access standards, so owners' rights would not be fully usable until well after enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For drivers, the upside is substantial: control over where-you-go and how-you-drive data that is currently collected and sold largely without meaningful consent, plus a right-to-repair-style guarantee of free access to one's own vehicle data. The main costs fall on automakers and data brokers, which is the point of the bill. The genuine design tradeoffs are the broad 'performance or safety' loophole, the override of stronger state privacy laws, and the lack of any private right of action — all fixable, but real. On balance the protections outweigh the costs for ordinary vehicle owners.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never came back out; the Congress ended and the bill died with it.

narrative.text: Representative Eric Burlison introduced the Auto Data Privacy and Autonomy Act on December 18, 2024, with Representative Andy Biggs as its one cosponsor.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is where bills affecting the FTC and communications policy are handled.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and the vehicle-data industry are better off because the bill died: connected vehicles continue generating, collecting, and selling driver data under whatever rules existed before, with no consent requirement, no foreign-adversary sales ban, and no owner right to free access.

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the sole cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (chair and members)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded; the bill's only support was two Republican House members, and no member is on record in opposition.

industries.note: Connected cars and trucks generate a constant stream of location, driving-behavior, and device data that manufacturers currently collect and monetize. The bill would require consent for access, bar most sales of that data, ban sales to five adversarial governments, and force manufacturers to give owners free, open access to their own vehicle data at the manufacturers' expense.

industries.industry: Telematics data brokers and the insurers/marketers that buy driver data
industries.note: These firms depend on vehicle data sold or shared by manufacturers — including driving-behavior data used to set insurance rates. The bill would cut off most of that supply by requiring owner consent before any sale or sharing.

industries.industry: Independent auto repair shops and aftermarket tools makers
industries.note: By requiring manufacturers to provide owners free, technology-neutral access to vehicle data without proprietary decryption fees or manufacturer-only devices, the bill would make it easier for owners to have their vehicles diagnosed and repaired outside the dealer network.
